content: The ulna, also known as the elbow bone, is a long, prismatic bone located on the medial side of the forearm. It runs parallel to the radius. The ulna forms articulations with several structures: It articulates with the humerus at the elbow joint, functioning as a hinge joint. It articulates with the radius near the elbow, forming a pivot joint. This allows the radius to cross over the ulna during pronation. It articulates with the distal radius, fitting into the ulnar notch. Along its length, the ulna is connected to the radius via the interosseous membrane, which forms a syndesmosis joint. The ulna is broader at its proximal end and narrows distally. Proximally, the ulna features the olecranon process, a hook-like bony structure that fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus. This structure prevents hyperextension and forms a hinge joint with the trochlea of the humerus. The proximal ulna also has a radial notch, which accommodates the head of the radius, and an ulnar tuberosity, which serves as an attachment site for muscles. Distally, near the hand, the ulna terminates in a styloid process. The structure of the ulna includes a long, narrow medullary cavity surrounded by a strong wall of compact bone. This compact bone is thickest along the interosseous border and the dorsal surface. At the extremities, the compact bone layer becomes thinner. The compact bone extends onto the posterior surface of the olecranon as a plate of dense spongy bone with parallel lamellae. From the inner surface of this plate and the compact bone beneath it, trabeculae arch forward toward the olecranon and coronoid processes. These trabeculae intersect with others that extend backward over the medullary cavity from the upper part of the shaft below the coronoid process. Below the coronoid process, there is a small area of compact bone from which trabeculae curve upward and terminate obliquely at the surface of the semilunar notch. This notch is coated with a thin layer of compact bone. At the lower end of the ulna, the trabeculae are oriented more longitudinally.
